about: Preparing for Patients A (PfP A) is the first-year part of Cambridge's Preparing for Patients strand, which gives preclinical medical students early contact with patients in general practice. According to the most recent official leaflet that could be opened (2022–23), it runs over the first two terms, with a preparation session, two GP visits in pairs (short surgery interviews and an hour-long home visit) and a final session watching GPs interview a patient, covering disease and illness, communication, confidentiality and consent. That leaflet describes two short written pieces, commented on by a GP tutor without a numerical mark, which must be submitted (and passed) for the 2nd MB; the Faculty's undated exam-structure page lists PfP A as 2nd MB coursework with reports handed in at Lent Term review sessions. Arrangements may have changed since 2022–23, so check the current course handbook and Moodle page.
topics: What Preparing for Patients A involves and how it is assessed

notes.h: What Preparing for Patients A is
notes.body:
Preparing for Patients (PfP) is the part of the Cambridge undergraduate medical course that gives students regular contact with real patients before clinical school. The 2022–23 leaflet says students take four PfP modules over their three undergraduate years; Module A is the first-year module. It sits within the Year 1 "Preparing for Clinical Practice" strand and is closely linked to the Social and Ethical Context of Health and Illness course.

What happens (based on the most recent official leaflet that could be opened, 2022–23)
- It runs over the first two terms of the first year.
- There is a preparation session that introduces guidelines for meeting patients and a framework for making sense of what you hear.
- You visit a general practice once each term, so twice in total. One visit involves short interviews with patients in the surgery; the other is an hour-long home visit to a patient.
- You work in pairs: one student interviews while the other observes, takes notes on how the conversation went and then gives feedback. A GP tutor supports you.
- A final session lets the group watch two GPs interview a patient, followed by a chance to ask questions and share experiences.

What it covers
- The difference between disease (the biomedical problem) and illness (the person's experience of being unwell).
- Communication and listening skills.
- Confidentiality and informed consent.
- Handling difficult moments, such as strong emotion, silence or a language barrier.

How it is assessed
- PfP A is assessed by coursework rather than an exam. You submit two short pieces of written work online at different stages; your GP tutor reads and comments on them, but they are not given a numerical mark.
- The 2022–23 leaflet says the pieces must be submitted and passed to meet the 2nd MB requirement, so you must complete them to progress. The Faculty's (undated) examination structure page lists PfP A as coursework assessed at 2nd MB level, with reports handed in at the Lent Term review sessions.
- No word limits were confirmed on the official pages, so check the current course handbook or Moodle page for deadlines, length and submission details.

Why it matters
- Most of Part IA is laboratory and lecture science. PfP is where you first link that science to real people, and practise skills you will use throughout clinical training.
- Because there is no mark, it is easy to treat it as a box-ticking exercise. But tutors' comments are valuable feedback, and failing to submit can hold up your progression.

Exam tips: there is no written exam for PfP A, so "preparing" means attending every session, keeping notes straight after each visit, and submitting both pieces on time.

notes.h: The medical interview and the patient's experience of illness
notes.body:
The core skill in PfP A is listening to a patient's story. You are not taking a full clinical history or making a diagnosis; you are learning how illness affects a person's life and how to talk with someone in a way that helps them tell you.

Disease and illness
- Disease is the doctor's account: abnormal structure or function that can be measured and named.
- Illness is the patient's account: how symptoms feel, what the person thinks is wrong, how it affects their work, family and identity, and what they fear.
- The two do not always match. A person can have a disease with no sense of illness (for example, high blood pressure found on screening), or feel very ill with no disease found. Good doctors attend to both.

A practical structure for an interview
- Prepare: know who you are seeing, check where to sit, turn off distractions.
- Introduce yourself clearly as a first-year medical student, explain the purpose of the conversation and check the patient is happy to talk (see the consent note).
- Start open: "Can you tell me about your health and how it has been for you?" Then let the patient talk without interrupting too early.
- Use active listening: eye contact, nodding, short encouragers ("go on"), and summarising back what you heard to check understanding.
- Move from open to more focused questions when you need detail.
- Explore the patient's ideas, concerns and expectations (often shortened to ICE): what they think is causing the problem, what worries them, and what they hope will happen.
- Ask about the effect on daily life, relationships, mood and work.
- Close: summarise, thank the patient and ask if there is anything they would like to add.
- Widely used frameworks such as the Calgary–Cambridge guide organise interviews into stages (initiating the session, gathering information, physical examination, explanation and planning, and closing), with building the relationship and providing structure running throughout. Your course may present its own version.

Handling difficult moments
- Silence: allow it; it often means the person is thinking or about to say something important.
- Strong emotion: acknowledge it ("this sounds really hard"), pause, and offer to stop or take a break. You do not need to fix it.
- Language barriers: speak simply, check understanding and do not rely on family members for sensitive topics; in clinical practice professional interpreters are used.
- Topics beyond your role: if a patient asks for medical advice or tells you something worrying about their safety, say you are a student and pass it on to your GP tutor.

Working as an interviewer and observer pair
- As observer, note specific behaviours and their effects (for example, "when you asked about work, she opened up").
- Give feedback that is specific, balanced and about behaviour, not personality. As interviewer, accept feedback openly.

Exam tips: in your written work, show that you noticed the patient's own perspective and link it to something you are learning in the science courses.

notes.h: Consent and confidentiality when meeting patients as a student
notes.body:
Meeting patients as a student raises the same ethical principles that govern all of medicine. PfP A introduces them in a practical setting. In the UK, the General Medical Council (GMC) publishes guidance that applies to doctors and, through its guidance for medical students, to students too.

Consent to take part
- Patients are never obliged to see a student. They must agree freely, knowing who you are and why you are there, and can change their mind at any time without it affecting their care.
- Always introduce yourself as a medical student, not as a doctor, and correct anyone who assumes otherwise.
- For a home visit, follow the practice's arrangements and your tutor's instructions about safety and who knows where you are.

Consent in clinical care (background: general UK law and guidance, not confirmed PfP A course content)
- The GMC's guidance "Decision making and consent" (in effect since November 2020) describes consent as a dialogue in which patients are given the information they want or need to make decisions about their care.
- In Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11, the UK Supreme Court held that doctors must take reasonable care to make patients aware of any material risks of a proposed treatment and of reasonable alternatives. A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would attach significance to it, or if the doctor knows (or should know) that this particular patient would.
- In England and Wales, the Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies to people aged 16 and over. Its section 1 principles are: a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it; they are not to be treated as unable to decide unless all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success; they are not to be treated as unable to decide merely because they make an unwise decision; anything done for a person who lacks capacity must be in their best interests; and before acting, consider whether the purpose can be achieved in a way less restrictive of their rights and freedom. Under sections 2 and 3, a person lacks capacity for a decision if, because of an impairment or disturbance in the functioning of the mind or brain, they cannot understand the relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it, or communicate their decision. Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate.

Confidentiality
- Patients share information on the understanding that it will be kept confidential. As background, the GMC's guidance "Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information" (in effect since 2017 and updated since) sets out when information may be shared, for example with consent, for direct care, or when required by law or justified in the public interest.
- As a student, you should never discuss patients in public places (corridors, buses, social media), and should not take photographs or keep identifiable notes.
- In written work, anonymise fully: no names, initials, dates of birth, addresses or other details that could identify the patient, such as an unusual occupation combined with a location.
- Store any notes securely and destroy them when they are no longer needed.

When confidentiality and safety conflict
- If a patient tells you something that suggests they or someone else is at risk of serious harm, do not promise to keep it secret. Explain that you will need to tell your GP tutor, and do so promptly.

Professionalism
- Dress and behave appropriately, arrive on time and thank patients for their time. Reflect on your own reactions; it is normal to find some conversations upsetting, and tutors and your college can support you.

Exam tips: in your reports, state how you obtained consent and how you anonymised the patient; this shows professional awareness even when the focus of the piece is elsewhere.

notes.h: Writing your reports and preparing for visits
notes.body:
PfP A's written work is short and unmarked, but it is compulsory for 2nd MB and it is the main record of what you learned. Treat it as practice for the reflective writing you will do throughout your medical career.

Before each visit
- Re-read the preparation session material and any guidance on Moodle.
- Agree with your partner who will interview and who will observe, and what each of you wants to practise.
- Plan a few open opening questions and prompts for exploring ideas, concerns and expectations, but be prepared to follow the patient's lead.
- Check travel arrangements and contact details for the practice.

Straight after each visit
- Write brief notes while it is fresh: what the patient said about their illness, how it affected their life, what went well in the conversation, what was difficult and what feedback you gave or received.
- Keep notes anonymised from the start.

Structuring a reflective piece
- One common structure is Gibbs' reflective cycle (1988): description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion and action plan. Another simple version is "What? So what? Now what?".
- Description: briefly and anonymously describe the patient and the situation. Keep this short; reflection matters more than narrative.
- Analysis: what did you learn about the patient's experience of illness compared with the disease? Which communication skills helped or hindered? How did the patient's ideas and concerns shape their behaviour?
- Linking to the course: connect what you heard with something from Part IA science where it genuinely fits, for example the biochemistry of diabetes in a patient living with the condition, or the anatomy behind a joint problem affecting mobility.
- Action: what will you do differently next time? Be specific.

Common pitfalls
- Writing a case history instead of a reflection.
- Including identifying details.
- Making clinical judgements beyond a first-year student's role (for example, criticising treatment).
- Missing the submission deadline; because submission is a 2nd MB requirement, late or missing work can create problems.

How to get the most from it
- Read and act on your GP tutor's comments.
- Use the final session, where you watch experienced GPs interview a patient, to compare their techniques with yours.
- Keep your reflections; they are useful later when you build a portfolio.

Exam tips: check the current course handbook or Moodle page for exact deadlines, length and format, because these details were not confirmed on the public official pages.

cards.f: How many GP practice visits in PfP A?
cards.b: Two, one per term in the first two terms of Year 1: one with short surgery interviews and one hour-long home visit (2022–23 leaflet).
Two short written pieces submitted online, commented on by a GP tutor with no numerical mark; they must be submitted and passed for 2nd MB (2022–23 leaflet).
Disease: the biomedical abnormality the doctor identifies. Illness: the patient's experience of being unwell and its effect on their life.
Ideas, concerns and expectations: what the patient thinks is wrong, what worries them and what they hope will happen.
Open questions invite a free answer ('Tell me about…'); closed questions seek specific facts (yes/no). Start open, then focus.

cards.f: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11
cards.b: Supreme Court: doctors must take reasonable care to tell patients about material risks and reasonable alternatives; materiality judged from the patient's perspective.

cards.f: Four abilities in the Mental Capacity Act 2005 test
cards.b: Understand the relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it, and communicate the decision (MCA 2005 s3; applies in England and Wales).

cards.f: Can a patient refuse to see a medical student?
cards.b: Yes. Patients must agree freely and can decline or withdraw at any time without affecting their care.
Description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan.

questions.q: During a home visit, a patient mentions something that makes you worried that a child in the household is at risk of harm. What should you do?
options: Promise to keep it secret, as patient confidentiality is absolute
Contact the police yourself before speaking to anyone else
Write it in your coursework report so the tutor sees it later
Explain that you cannot keep this confidential and inform your GP tutor promptly
questions.why: Confidentiality is not absolute when someone may be at risk of serious harm, and as a student your duty is to tell your supervising GP tutor promptly so that those responsible can act. Promising secrecy is wrong because it cannot be kept and treats confidentiality as absolute. Contacting the police yourself bypasses the GP, who is responsible for the patient and for safeguarding decisions. Saving it for your coursework report would delay action and would put identifiable, sensitive information into written work.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the law on consent to treatment in the UK after Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board (2015)?
options: Doctors must make patients aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives, judged from the patient's perspective
Doctors need disclose only the risks that a responsible body of doctors would disclose
Consent is valid only if given in writing
Patients must accept their doctor's recommended treatment
questions.why: Montgomery moved the standard of disclosure to what a reasonable person in the patient's position (or this particular patient) would consider significant. Basing disclosure on what other doctors would disclose was the earlier approach it replaced; consent need not be written to be valid; and patients with capacity can refuse recommended treatment.

questions.q: Explain the difference between disease and illness, and describe two interview techniques that help a student understand a patient's experience of illness.
markScheme: Disease: biomedical abnormality that can be measured and named
Illness: the patient's subjective experience and its impact on their life; the two may not match
Technique 1, e.g. open questions and allowing the patient to speak without interruption
Technique 2, e.g. exploring ideas, concerns and expectations, active listening and summarising
questions.modelAnswer: Disease is the biomedical account of what is wrong: a structural or functional abnormality that can be measured, diagnosed and named. Illness is the patient's own experience of being unwell, including symptoms, worries and the effect on work, family and identity; the two do not always match, as when someone has silent high blood pressure or feels very unwell with no disease found. To understand illness, a student should start with open questions, such as asking the patient to describe how their health has affected them, and let them talk without interrupting too early. Exploring their ideas, concerns and expectations, and summarising back what they said, shows that the student is listening and helps the patient say what matters to them.
